newsitem.title: GERMANY: German media see gaps on Euro bank strategy.
newsitem.headline: German media see gaps on Euro bank strategy.

text.p: This week's long awaited report by the European Monetary Institute on the toolkit to be used by the future European Central Bank left key strategic questions unanswered, the German media observed on Saturday.

"Whoever hoped for anything decisive from the EMI on central questions on future European monetary policy will be disappointed," the respected Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung said in an editorial comment.

"As the forerunner to the European Central Bank, the institution (the EMI) is no more than a reflection of the interests of all national central banks and their monetary traditions," the newspaper added.

The EMI on Friday revealed a toolkit for the bank which will guide Europe's monetary policy once the Euro is launched, as planned, in January 1999, but fell short of finalising an overall strategy for the bank, or decide if it would require banks to hold minimum reserves with it, as the Bundesbank does.

The Sueddeutsche Zeitung praised EMI President Alexandre Lamfalussy as a "true diplomat" for skilfully deflecting charges that the agreement so far on the ECB's policy-making framework was less than significant.
"The true diplomat always has a statement ready, even if the significance of that statement is virtually nil ... Alexandre Lamfalussy is one of these...," the newspaper said.
Nonetheless, the Sueddeutsche praised the spirit of openness which sparked the publication of the plans for the ECB, which was not required by the Maastricht Treaty.

"If the European Central Bank takes on the task of keeping banks, financial markets, politicians and citizens informed on its activities to the best of its ability, then one goal will already be achieved," the paper said.
Die Welt newspaper took a more positive line in its commentary, noting that the framework was in place for a future European monetary policy, even if many details had yet to be finalised.

The newspaper, however, warned of the dangers of ignoring the imminent arrival of the Euro, noting that only banks and the most internationally-oriented companies in Germany were preparing for the 1999 start date.
"A forward-looking businessman cannot afford this stance," Die Welt said.
